title: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
summary: What open source licenses permit and require, when copyleft obliges you to share source, which licenses can be combined, and how CLAs and the DCO sign-off govern the code you contribute.
outcomes: Explain why code without a license cannot be reused, and list what MIT and Apache-2.0 require on redistribution
Predict whether shipping, internal use or a hosted service triggers a source obligation under GPL-3.0 and AGPL-3.0
Decide whether code under one license can be combined into a project under another, including GPLv2 and GPLv3
Explain inbound=outbound and what an individual or corporate CLA grants
Add and fix DCO sign-offs, and diagnose a failing DCO or CLA check on a pull request

lessons.title: No license means no permission: what a license grants

blocks.md:
Code is a creative work, so it is under **exclusive copyright** the moment it is written. Without a license, nobody else can copy, distribute or modify it without risking a takedown or a lawsuit ([choosealicense: No License](https://choosealicense.com/no-permission/)). Publishing a public repository on GitHub only grants what GitHub's terms say: others may view and fork it there.

An **open source license** is the copyright holder's written permission to use, copy, modify and redistribute the code, given to everyone, usually with conditions attached.

blocks.prompt: You find a useful public GitHub repository with no LICENSE file. Can your company copy one of its functions into a product it ships?
blocks.reveal: **No.** No license means the default applies: all rights reserved. The GitHub terms let people view and fork the repository on GitHub, which is not permission to ship the code elsewhere. The fix is to ask the author to add a license (choosealicense even shows how to suggest one politely), or to write your own code.

blocks.md:
Every license can be read as three lists, which is how choosealicense.com (maintained by GitHub) presents them:

- **Permissions**: what you may do (commercial use, distribution, modification, private use, sometimes patent use).
- **Conditions**: what you must do *if* you exercise a permission, such as keep the copyright notice.
- **Limitations**: what the license does not give you (no warranty, no liability, sometimes no trademark rights).

The conditions are where licenses differ most, so count them first.

blocks.title: Conditions listed per license on choosealicense.com

scenes.caption: Count of conditions each license page lists. MIT has one: keep the license and copyright notice. Apache-2.0 adds 'state changes' (mark files you modified).
Permissive licenses (MIT, Apache-2.0) stop at notices. Choosealicense says works using them 'may be distributed under different terms and without source code'.

Copyleft licenses add 'disclose source' and 'same license'. MPL-2.0 scopes that to files, LGPL-3.0 to the library, GPL-3.0 to the whole work, and AGPL-3.0 adds network use. Lesson 2 covers when these trigger.

blocks.md:
**MIT** is a few sentences: permission to "use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and/or sell" the software, on one condition: "The above copyright notice and this permission notice shall be included in all copies or substantial portions of the Software." The rest is a warranty disclaimer.

**Apache-2.0** section 4 asks four things when you redistribute: (a) give recipients a copy of the license, (b) make modified files carry prominent notices that you changed them, (c) keep the copyright, patent, trademark and attribution notices, and (d) pass on the attribution notices from a `NOTICE` file if the project has one. You may license your own modifications, or the larger work as a whole, under different terms.

Apache-2.0 also has an **express patent grant** (section 3). Each contributor licenses any of their patents that their contribution necessarily infringes. If you sue anyone claiming the Work infringes a patent, the patent licenses you received for that Work terminate on the day you file. MIT has no such clause, which is why the FSF recommends Apache-2.0 over other permissive licenses for substantial programs.
Public is not the same as open source. Code you can read on GitHub with no license file is all rights reserved, and so is a snippet whose license you never checked.
A license is permission plus conditions. The conditions only apply when you do the thing they attach to, which for most licenses means distributing the code.

blocks.question: You modify two files of an Apache-2.0 library and ship it inside a closed-source desktop app. Which of these does Apache-2.0 require?
options: Publish the source of your app, since it contains Apache code
Nothing, because Apache-2.0 has no conditions on binaries
Include the license, mark the two files as changed, keep the existing notices and the NOTICE attributions
Get written permission from the Apache Software Foundation
blocks.explain: Section 4 lists exactly these conditions. Apache-2.0 is permissive: section 4 lets you put the larger work under your own terms, and nothing requires releasing source. The conditions do apply to binaries too: recipients must get a copy of the license.

blocks.question: Your company uses an Apache-2.0 library and later files a patent suit claiming that library infringes one of its patents. What happens under section 3?
options: The patent licenses your company received for that library terminate as of the filing date
The copyright license terminates and you must stop using the code
Nothing, because Apache-2.0 only covers copyright
The library's contributors lose their own patents
blocks.explain: Section 3 grants a patent license from each contributor, and it terminates for anyone who starts patent litigation alleging the Work infringes. The copyright license in section 2 is not what terminates.

lessons.title: Copyleft: when you must share source, and with whom

blocks.md:
**Copyleft** licenses let you do everything a permissive license does, on one bigger condition: when you pass the software on, you pass on the same freedoms, including the source code. GPLv3 section 5(c) says you must "license the entire work, as a whole, under this License to anyone who comes into possession of a copy."

The key word is **convey**. GPLv3 defines it as "any kind of propagation that enables other parties to make or receive copies" and adds: "Mere interaction with a user through a computer network, with no transfer of a copy, is not conveying."

So the obligations hang on what you do with the code:

- **Use and modify privately** (one person or a whole company in-house): not conveying, so no obligation. The FSF's GPL FAQ says an organization "can make a modified version and use it internally without ever releasing it outside the organization."
- **Ship a binary** (app download, device firmware): conveying. Section 6 requires the machine-readable *Corresponding Source* alongside, or a written offer, or access from the same place.
- **Run it as a service**: not conveying under the GPL. The AGPL closes this gap in section 13: if you *modify* the program, users who interact with it remotely must be offered your version's source.

scenes.caption: Using or modifying code privately triggers no source duty under MIT, Apache-2.0 or GPL-3.0, since nothing is conveyed. AGPL-3.0 is an edge case: section 13 covers all remote users of a modified version, which can include staff.
Shipping a binary is conveying. MIT and Apache-2.0 need only notices; GPL-3.0 and AGPL-3.0 need the Corresponding Source for recipients (GPLv3 section 6).
A web service conveys no copy, so GPL-3.0 adds no duty. AGPL-3.0 section 13 does, for a modified version: remote users must be offered its source.
Simplified: rules encoded from the license texts. Real cases also hinge on what counts as one combined work, covered next.

blocks.md: Who receives the source? Only the people you convey to, not the whole world. The GPL FAQ: "if you release the modified version to the public in some way, the GPL requires you to make the modified source code available to the program's users." Copyleft also does not forbid selling: choosealicense lists commercial use as a permission of GPL-3.0.

What does the "whole work" include? GPLv3 separates a combined program from an **aggregate**: separate, independent works placed on the same medium. Including a GPL program in an aggregate "does not cause this License to apply to the other parts."

The line between two programs and one program with two parts is ultimately legal, but the FSF's stated view is concrete: modules in the same executable, or designed to run linked in a shared address space, are one program; pipes, sockets and command-line arguments normally connect separate programs.

blocks.title: One combined work or two separate programs?

scenes.caption: Your code links a GPL-3.0 library into one executable. In the FSF's view that is one program, so shipping it means licensing the whole thing under GPL-3.0.
Instead, your code starts a separate GPL tool and talks to it over a pipe. Pipes and arguments normally connect two separate programs.
Shipping both side by side on one medium forms an aggregate: the tool keeps its GPL terms and your code keeps yours (GPLv3 section 5).
Simplified: the FSF criterion also weighs what data the parts exchange, and courts decide edge cases. Weak copyleft (LGPL, MPL) narrows the scope instead.

blocks.md: **Weak copyleft** narrows what "the work" means. LGPL-3.0: a larger work that uses the library through the library's interfaces may be distributed under different terms and without its own source, as long as users can still replace the library with a modified version (LGPL-3.0 section 4). MPL-2.0 is file-level: modified MPL files stay MPL and their source must be available, while files you add to a larger work may use other terms.

blocks.prompt: A startup modifies an AGPL-3.0 database and offers it to customers as a hosted service; it never ships the code. Would anything change if the database were GPL-3.0 instead?
blocks.reveal: Yes. Under **GPL-3.0** nothing is owed: serving users over a network is not conveying. Under **AGPL-3.0** section 13, the modified version must "prominently offer all users interacting with it remotely" a way to get its Corresponding Source from a network server at no charge. That one clause is why some companies ban AGPL dependencies in hosted products.

blocks.md: Two common myths: copyleft does not make internal use public (only conveying triggers it), and it does not ban commercial use (you may charge for copies). What it controls is the terms you pass on.
Copyleft obligations trigger on conveying: giving someone a copy. AGPL is the exception that also counts remote network use of a modified version.

blocks.question: A bank modifies a GPL-3.0 command-line tool and runs it on internal servers only. An employee asks for the modified source to publish on GitHub. What does the license require?
options: The bank must publish the source within a reasonable time
Nothing: in-house use is not conveying, so no source obligation arises
The bank must give the source to that employee only
The bank must switch to the AGPL
blocks.explain: Using a program inside one organization is not conveying, and the GPL FAQ confirms an organization can use a modified version internally without releasing it. Obligations start only when copies go to others.

blocks.question: Which change to a proprietary app is most likely to pull it under GPL-3.0 terms when shipped?
options: Calling a GPL-3.0 command-line tool through a pipe
Putting a GPL-3.0 tool on the same installer as a separate program
Statically linking a GPL-3.0 library into the app's executable
Reading a file format that a GPL-3.0 program also reads
blocks.explain: Code in the same executable is one program in the FSF's view, and GPLv3 section 5(c) then covers the whole work. Pipes and aggregates keep programs separate, and a file format is not code you copied.

lessons.title: License compatibility: can these two pieces of code be combined?

blocks.md: When you copy code into your project, or link it into one program, you need to satisfy **both** licenses at once. The FSF's GPL FAQ defines it: two licenses are compatible if they permit combining the programs into a larger work; "if there is no way to satisfy both licenses at once, they are incompatible." Installing two programs side by side needs no compatibility, because nothing is combined.

Start small. Four project licenses, five sources of code. For each pair ask: can the combined work be distributed as a whole under the project's license, with every piece's conditions still met? The rules come from the license texts and the two organizations that wrote them:

- MIT allows anything as long as the notice travels with it.
- Apache-2.0 section 4 lets a larger work use other terms. The FSF lists Apache-2.0 as compatible with GPLv3 but not GPLv2, citing patent termination and indemnification requirements; the ASF agrees the one-way direction.
- GPL code requires the whole to be GPL, and GPLv2 and GPLv3 are not compatible with each other.

blocks.title: Can row code go into a work shipped under the column license?

scenes.caption: MIT code fits everywhere: every target license can carry its one condition, the notice. The diagonal is trivially 1.
Apache-2.0 code fits MIT, Apache and GPL-3.0 projects, but not GPL-2.0-only: its patent termination clause is an extra restriction GPLv2 does not allow.
GPL code only fits a project that is itself under that GPL version. GPL-2.0-only and GPL-3.0-only code cannot be combined in either direction.
'GPL-2.0-or-later' code lets the recipient pick v2 or v3, so it fits both GPL projects. That one clause is why many projects avoid 'only'.
Simplified: 1 assumes you also meet the source's own conditions (notices, NOTICE file). Read columns as 'what this project can accept'.

blocks.md: Read the matrix as a contributor: before you paste code from Stack Overflow, a blog or another repository into a project, check its license against the project's column. The Linux kernel is a concrete case. Its licensing rules say the kernel is under "GPL-2.0" (version 2 only) with a syscall exception, and individual files may use other licenses only if they are compatible with GPL-2.0, such as GPL-2.0+ or a dual license with a permissive one.

Projects make licenses machine-readable with **SPDX identifiers**, short standard names from the SPDX License List such as `MIT`, `Apache-2.0` and `GPL-2.0-or-later`. The kernel requires one on the first possible comment line of each file:

- C source: `// SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0`
- scripts (second line, after the shebang): `# SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0`

The kernel's `GPL-2.0` is the older SPDX spelling of `GPL-2.0-only`. An expression joined with `OR` marks a dual-licensed file where the recipient picks one license.

blocks.prompt: A GPL-3.0 project wants to vendor a 300-line helper licensed GPL-2.0-or-later. A second helper is GPL-2.0-only. Which ones can it take?
blocks.reveal: The **GPL-2.0-or-later** helper is fine: "or any later version" lets the project use it under GPLv3. The **GPL-2.0-only** helper is not: the FSF states the two versions are incompatible, and combining them would violate section 6 of GPLv2. Asking its authors to relicense is the only clean fix.

blocks.md: When you open a PR, the project's license is the column. Code you wrote yourself is fine; code you copied needs a row that is 1 in that column, with its notices kept.

Compatibility is about combining code into one work. Permissive code flows into almost anything; copyleft code only flows into the same copyleft, and version clauses like 'only' and 'or later' decide which.

blocks.question: You want to copy an Apache-2.0 function into a Linux kernel driver (GPL-2.0-only). Which is correct?
options: Allowed, Apache-2.0 is permissive so it fits any project
Allowed, if you keep the NOTICE file
Not allowed as is: the FSF does not consider Apache-2.0 compatible with GPLv2
Allowed, because the kernel has a syscall exception
blocks.explain: Apache-2.0 is compatible with GPLv3 only. Its patent termination and indemnification terms are restrictions GPLv2 does not permit, so a GPL-2.0-only work cannot absorb it. The syscall exception concerns user programs calling the kernel, not code inside it.

blocks.question: Which pair can be combined into one distributed program?
options: GPL-2.0-only code inside a GPL-3.0-only project
MIT code inside a GPL-2.0-only project
GPL-3.0 code inside an Apache-2.0 project that stays Apache-2.0
Apache-2.0 code inside a GPL-2.0-only project
blocks.explain: MIT is GPL-compatible: its only condition is keeping the notice, which any GPL version allows. The other three either mix incompatible GPL versions, need the whole to become GPL, or add restrictions GPLv2 forbids.

lessons.title: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements

blocks.md: So far we looked at **outbound** licensing: the terms a project gives its users. When you send a pull request, the reverse question appears. Under what terms does the project receive *your* code? That is **inbound** licensing, and a maintainer needs a clear answer before they can ship your change under the project's license.

The default answer is **inbound=outbound**: you contribute under the same license the project uses. Apache-2.0 writes this into section 5: unless you explicitly state otherwise, a contribution you intentionally submit "shall be under the terms and conditions of this License." GitHub's Terms of Service do the same for any repository with a license notice (section D.6), adding that a separate agreement such as a contributor license agreement supersedes it.

A **contributor license agreement (CLA)** is that separate agreement, signed once before your first contribution is accepted. The Apache ICLA and Google's Individual CLA share the same core:

1. A perpetual, worldwide, royalty-free, irrevocable **copyright license** to the project owner and to recipients of its software.
2. A **patent license** for your patent claims that your contribution necessarily infringes, terminated for anyone who sues claiming it infringes.
3. **Representations**: you are legally entitled to grant this, and if your employer has rights to your work, it gave permission or signed a corporate CLA.

You keep ownership: both say you "reserve all right, title, and interest" in your contributions.

blocks.title: Who grants what to whom when you contribute

scenes.caption: Outbound: the project licenses the software to users, say under Apache-2.0. This is the license you see in the LICENSE file.
Inbound=outbound: your PR is licensed to the project under that same license (Apache-2.0 section 5, GitHub terms D.6). No paperwork.
With a CLA you sign once, granting copyright and patent licenses to the owner and its recipients. You still own your code.
If your employer owns what you write, your representations depend on it: it must permit you or sign a corporate CLA (CCLA) naming who may contribute.

blocks.md: Projects differ in when they require it. The ASF: small contributions arrive under clause 5 of Apache-2.0, but committers and contributors of large contributions must sign an ICLA, and a corporate CLA "does not remove the need for every developer to sign their own ICLA." Google: it checks every contribution and will not accept one without a CLA on file. Under a Google CCLA, your organization lists authorized contributors by email in a Google Group, so commit with that email (`git config user.email`) and add it to your GitHub account.

blocks.title: First PR to a project that requires a CLA

scenes.caption: You open a pull request. The project's CLA check looks up the commit email against agreements on file.
No agreement matches, so the check fails and the PR cannot be accepted yet. The project will not accept it until the check passes.
You sign the individual CLA once (or your employer adds your email to its CCLA group).
On recheck the email now matches, the check passes, and normal review begins. Later PRs from the same email pass directly.

blocks.md: The most common CLA failure is an email mismatch: the commits use a personal or unregistered address while the agreement (or the employer's group) lists another. Fix the author email and rewrite the commits, not the agreement.

Outbound is what users get; inbound is what the project gets from you. Inbound=outbound needs no paperwork; a CLA is a one-time signed grant, often with an explicit patent license and a statement about your employer.

blocks.question: Your employer signed Google's corporate CLA, yet the CLA check on your PR fails. What is the most likely cause?
options: Corporate CLAs only cover Google employees
Your commit email is not in the employer's authorized contributor group or not linked to your GitHub account
The project uses inbound=outbound, so CLAs are ignored
You must also assign copyright to Google
blocks.explain: Google maps contributions to a CCLA through the email addresses in the organization's group, and asks contributors to use that address in git and on GitHub. The CLA grants a license; you keep ownership.

blocks.question: A one-line typo fix to an Apache project arrives from someone with no ICLA. Under what terms does the ASF receive it?
options: It cannot be accepted until an ICLA is signed
Under Apache-2.0 section 5, as small contributions are
Under no terms: the ASF must rewrite it
Under the contributor's employer's license
blocks.explain: The ASF states that small contributions are made under clause 5 of Apache-2.0; ICLAs are required for committers and for large contributions.

lessons.title: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by

blocks.md:
The **Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO)** is the lightweight alternative to a CLA. Nothing is signed in advance and no rights are granted beyond the project's license (inbound=outbound still applies). Instead, each commit carries a line certifying where the code came from. Its text is copyright the Linux Foundation, and the git-commit docs name it as the one the Linux kernel and Git projects use.

DCO 1.1 says that by making a contribution, I certify that:

- **(a)** I created it, in whole or in part, and have the right to submit it under the open source license indicated in the file; or
- **(b)** it is based on previous work that, to the best of my knowledge, is under an appropriate open source license that lets me submit it with my changes under that same license (unless I am permitted to use a different one); or
- **(c)** someone who certified (a), (b) or (c) gave it to me directly and I did not modify it.
- **(d)** I understand and agree that the project and the contribution are public, and that a record of it, including my sign-off and personal details, is kept indefinitely and may be redistributed.

You certify this by adding a trailer, `Signed-off-by: Your Name <you@example.org>`. `git commit -s` (`--signoff`) adds it using your configured name and email. The kernel adds: use a known identity, "no anonymous contributions."

blocks.code:
git config user.name  "Ada Dev"
git config user.email ada@example.org
git commit -s -m "Add parser"

# resulting message:
# Add parser
#
# Signed-off-by: Ada Dev <ada@example.org>
blocks.caption: Git deliberately has no config option to sign off by default; the git-commit docs point to the gitfaq for why. Pass -s each time.

blocks.md: On GitHub, many DCO projects use the DCO app (Probot DCO). Per its README it requires every commit in a PR to contain a `Signed-off-by` line "with an email address that matches the commit author," skipping bots and merges, and blocks the PR until fixed. The trace below re-implements that core rule and runs it on a real three-commit branch.

blocks.title: A minimal DCO check, run on three commits
blocks.code:
import re, subprocess

def commits(rng):
    fmt = "%h|%ae|%(trailers:key=Signed-off-by,valueonly,separator=;)"
    out = subprocess.run(["git", "log", "--reverse", "--format=" + fmt, rng],
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
    for line in out.strip().splitlines():
        yield line.split("|")

failed = 0
for sha, author, sob in commits("main..HEAD"):
    emails = re.findall(r"<([^>]+)>", sob)
    ok = author in emails
    print(sha, "PASS" if ok else "FAIL")
    failed += not ok
raise SystemExit(1 if failed else 0)

scenes.caption: List commits on the branch with author email and the Signed-off-by values Git parses from each message's trailers.
Commit 1ed77f0 was made with git commit -s, so its sign-off email equals the author email.
Commit 787b49b was made without -s. No trailer at all, so the check fails.
Commit fa021d0 was signed off by hand with a work address that differs from the author email. A sign-off exists but does not match, so it fails too.
Any failure gives a non-zero exit, which CI shows as a failed check. Simplified: the real app also handles bots, merges and remediation commits.

blocks.prompt: You run `git rebase --signoff main` on that branch. Which commit hashes change, and does the third commit pass afterwards?
blocks.reveal: All three hashes change. `--signoff` forces rebase to rewrite every commit on the branch, even the first, whose message stays the same (it already ends with your sign-off) but gets a new committer date. You then force-push the branch. The third commit now has two trailers, the old work address and a new `Signed-off-by` matching the author email, so it passes. Running it on the real repository confirms this.

blocks.title: The branch before and after git rebase --signoff

scenes.caption: Before: one valid sign-off, one missing, one with a mismatched email. The DCO app blocks the PR.
After git rebase --signoff: Git appends your sign-off where the last trailer is not already yours. --signoff forces a full rebase, so all three commits are rewritten and get new hashes.
Every commit now carries a sign-off matching its author, so the check passes. Force-push the branch to update the PR.

blocks.md:
Sign-offs also record the route a patch took. In the kernel the first `Signed-off-by` is the author; later ones are people who handled and forwarded it, and the last must be the person submitting it. Each `Co-developed-by:` must be followed immediately by that co-author's own `Signed-off-by:`, and reverts need a sign-off too (`git revert -s`).

Signing off is not signing: GitHub's docs separate a sign-off (a text trailer certifying the rules) from a cryptographic commit signature. GitHub can also require sign-off for commits made in its web interface; from the command line you add `--signoff` yourself.

Because the DCO is a personal certification, AI tools raise a new question. The kernel's AI coding assistants guide says AI agents "MUST NOT add Signed-off-by tags": only a human can certify the DCO, after reviewing the code, and tool use is credited with an `Assisted-by:` tag. QEMU goes further and declines contributions believed to include AI-generated content, because it is unclear how a contributor could satisfy clauses (b) or (c) for such output.

A sign-off you add without reading the DCO is still a legal statement about provenance. Copying code you cannot trace (a gist without a license, generated output in a project that bans it) and signing off is exactly what the DCO exists to prevent.
CLA: one signed agreement per person or company, granting rights up front. DCO: no agreement, just a per-commit certification of origin via Signed-off-by, checked mechanically by email match.

blocks.question: A DCO-checked PR has three commits. Which one fails?
options: Author ada@example.org, trailer Signed-off-by: Ada Dev <ada@example.org>
A merge commit from the main branch with no trailer
Author ada@example.org, trailer Signed-off-by: Ada Dev <ada@work.example>
Author ada@example.org with two trailers, one of them ada@example.org
blocks.explain: The DCO app requires a sign-off whose email matches the commit author. A mismatched address fails even though a sign-off exists. The app skips merge commits by default, and an extra trailer does not hurt if one matches.

blocks.question: A project wants contributor provenance with minimal friction for drive-by contributors, and does not need any rights beyond its license. Which fits best?
options: A corporate CLA with each contributor's employer
The DCO with a sign-off check on every commit
An individual CLA signed before any PR is reviewed
No policy, since inbound=outbound needs no record at all
blocks.explain: The DCO adds one trailer per commit and no paperwork, while still recording a certification of origin. CLAs suit projects that want an explicit, signed grant (often including patents); no policy leaves no record of who certified the code's origin.
